summary: This memo presents the set of protocols and procedures that make up Inter-Domain Policy Routing, which lets routes between networks follow policies. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This is the instruction manual for a system that picks routes between networks according to each network's rules. It is historic.

subtitle: Routes between networks according to each network's policies.

tldr.problem: Internet routing at the time used simple hop-count metrics that ignored network policies. Administrative domains needed a way to specify which domains they would allow traffic through, under what conditions, and with what service qualities.
tldr.mechanism: IDPR builds routes between administrative domains using policy information distributed by each domain, then sets up explicit paths across the Internet that respect those policies.
tldr.outcome: IDPR became historic because simpler policy-based approaches like BGP with route filters proved more practical for widespread deployment. The complex protocol machinery of IDPR did not see production use at Internet scale.

today: RFC 1479 is Historic. IDPR was designed in the early 1990s as a comprehensive solution to inter-domain policy routing, but did not achieve widespread deployment. Simpler approaches, particularly BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) with route filtering and policy extensions, proved more practical and became the standard for inter-domain routing.

sections.title: The Problem of Inter-Domain Routing
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, Internet routing between administrative domains (organizations, networks, or service providers) operated without any way to express policy. The IDPR specification describes a complete system for constructing and maintaining routes between source and destination domains according to the policies that each domain sets.

The core insight is that each administrative domain manages its own networks and links, and should be able to specify which services it offers to transit traffic, what access restrictions apply, and what service quality guarantees it can provide. Similarly, domains that originate traffic should be able to specify what service quality they require and which domains they prefer or exclude.

IDPR includes six complementary protocols: a control message transport protocol (CMTP), a virtual gateway protocol (VGP) to track connectivity between domains, a flooding protocol to distribute routing information, a route server query protocol, a route generation procedure, and a path control protocol that sets up explicit paths across the Internet.
sections.eli5: When you mail a package across the country, you have rules about which post offices can handle it (maybe some are too busy). IDPR is like a postal system where every post office tells all the others its rules, and they work together to find routes for your package.

sections.title: Domains, Virtual Gateways, and Policy Gateways
sections.content:
IDPR's architecture is built on three key concepts. An administrative domain (AD) is a collection of contiguous hosts, networks, and links managed by a single authority. Within and between domains are policy gateways (PGs) - the only IDPR-recognized connection points between adjacent domains. A collection of peer policy gateways in two adjacent domains that have mutual agreement to interconnect forms a virtual gateway (VG). Two domains may establish multiple virtual gateways between them.

Each domain administrator defines transit policies describing which service restrictions the domain will enforce on traffic passing through, and source policies describing the service requirements for traffic the domain generates. Policies include access restrictions (favoring or excluding certain domains), quality of service requirements (delay, throughput, reliability), and monetary cost constraints.

IDPR delegates all intra-domain details - which specific gateways and networks carry traffic - to intra-domain routing. IDPR itself operates at the inter-domain level, viewing routing as finding sequences of domains that provide the requested services.
sections.eli5: Think of each network as a city with gates (policy gateways) where traffic enters and exits. A link between two gates is a virtual gateway. Each city has rules about what traffic it will carry. IDPR uses these rules to plan routes across multiple cities.

sections.title: The Six Component Protocols
sections.content:
IDPR comprises six complementary protocols. The Control Message Transport Protocol (CMTP) is a connectionless, transaction-based transport that all IDPR protocols use. It provides message retransmission, timeout handling, and integrity/authentication checks using algorithms ranging from simple checksums to digital signatures. This was necessary because IDPR control messages must be reliably delivered to ensure correct route construction.

The Virtual Gateway Protocol (VGP) tracks connectivity changes between domains. Policy gateways exchange UP/DOWN messages to determine whether direct connections between them are usable, and propagate connectivity information (using Pair-PG, Intra-VG, and Inter-VG message types) so all policy gateways can maintain a consistent picture of virtual gateway status.

The Flooding Protocol distributes routing information (domain connectivity and transit policies) using link-state techniques similar to OSPF, with sequence numbers and configuration vs. dynamic message types. A Route Server Query Protocol allows path agents to ask route servers for routes matching specified service requirements. Route Generation uses distributed routing information to construct policy routes that respect transit policy restrictions. Finally, the Path Control Protocol sets up explicit paths across the Internet by exchanging SETUP, ACCEPT, REFUSE, and ERROR messages between domains, validating policies and managing path lifetimes.
sections.eli5: IDPR uses six specialized talking systems: a reliable messenger (CMTP), neighborhood status reporters (VGP), town bulletin boards (flooding), librarians who answer questions (route servers), map makers (route generation), and the main route builders (path control).

sections.title: Security, Timestamps, and Management
sections.content:
IDPR includes security measures critical for protecting control information. All IDPR control messages must carry a non-null integrity/authentication value computed using either symmetric algorithms (like checksums), asymmetric signature algorithms (like RSA applied to MD5), or other IANA-approved mechanisms. Domain administrators can select algorithms independently, and IDPR recommends entities be capable of executing all approved algorithms.

Data messages (user traffic) do not require IDPR-level integrity checks; higher-layer protocols are responsible for that. Each IDPR message carries a timestamp (seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC) to indicate message age. IDPR entities require clock synchronization to within minutes, which can be achieved manually. Messages outside acceptable time ranges are rejected.

IDPR defines configuration for domains to specify which integrity/authentication schemes, user classes, offered services (delay, bandwidth, cost), access restrictions, and requested services are valid. Each domain administrator develops this configuration using global information from the IANA, then distributes it to policy gateways and route servers via configuration servers (integrated with existing DNS and network management systems).
sections.eli5: Each message is sealed with a tamper-proof mark so cities know it hasn't been forged. Every message is time-stamped, and cities have to keep their clocks roughly together. City administrators register their rules with a central authority so all cities learn what each allows.

sections.title: Route Selection and Data Forwarding
sections.content:
When a source domain generates traffic, its path agent (a component in a policy gateway or route server) selects a policy route matching the source policy requirements, then initiates path setup. The source sends a SETUP message across the Internet, specifying the destination domain and service requirements. Each intermediate policy gateway validates the path against its transit policies, obtains any required resources, and either accepts or refuses the path. If all domains accept, the path is established and a forwarding database entry is created. Data messages carry a path identifier and are forwarded based on this database.

Path failures are handled through explicit repair messages rather than re-sending SETUP. The specification describes both local repair (where a failed domain tries to find an alternate path to the next domain) and end-to-end repair initiated by the source.

The document defines detailed message formats and state machines for all protocols, provides a complete example of path setup, and discusses edge cases like partitioned domains and path lifetime management.
sections.eli5: When someone sends a package, the sender's city asks all the cities along the route if they'll carry it. Each city checks its rules, then either says yes or no. If yes, they mark down which gates the package will use, then send the package along the agreed route.
